name: Regression toward the mean (height)

lead: Regression toward the mean describes how the children of unusually tall or short parents tend, on average, to be closer to the population average than their parents were. Paediatric endocrinologists pair it with the mid-parental height, a figure derived from both parents' heights, to give a target range for a growing child.

For people who want to understand their own height ceiling, it is the usual starting point for setting expectations before adding other information such as growth charts and bone age. Clinical reviews treat parental height as one of the standard predictors of growth outcomes, including how children respond to growth hormone therapy.

paras: Practitioners compare a child's measured height with the range predicted from the parents' heights and look at whether the child sits well above or below it. Forum users on height threads often quote their parents' heights alongside their own to estimate a potential. Doctors combine the figure with growth velocity and bone age.

The estimate is an average for a population, so individuals can fall well above or below it. In clinical practice, a child far outside their mid-parental range is typically referred for endocrine assessment, since some hormonal and genetic conditions change growth.

angle.text: The framework gives a baseline for adult height before any intervention. People use it to see whether their own growth is tracking their genetic target and to decide whether a doctor's assessment of growth is worthwhile.

lead: Regression toward the mean, in the context of height, is the observation that children of very tall parents are usually tall but on average less tall than their parents, while children of very short parents are usually short but on average taller than their parents. The pattern was first quantified by Francis Galton in 1886, who measured the heights of 930 adult children and their 205 sets of parents and described the result as regression toward mediocrity in hereditary stature.[1][2]

In clinical practice the idea is paired with the mid-parental height: a figure built from the mother's and father's heights, adjusted for the child's sex, that serves as a genetic target for a growing child. Paediatric reviews state that expected growth should be predicted from mid-parental height, a step they describe as often omitted.[3] Mid-parental height also appears in the definition of gigantism and in studies of how children respond to growth hormone therapy.[4][5]

In looksmaxxing and height-focused forums, people routinely post their parents' heights next to their own age and height to estimate their potential adult height, and the target-height calculation is the standard first reference point before any discussion of bone age, growth plates or other interventions.[6] Its use for appearance is expectation-setting: it tells a person where their growth is likely to end and whether their current trajectory sits inside or outside the expected range, which informs whether a clinical assessment, footwear or other height-adding options are worth considering.

paras: A child's height is influenced by inherited variants at hundreds of loci together with nutrition, health and other environmental factors, so a parent-to-child prediction is an average rather than a guarantee.[7] Offspring of extreme parents are expected to be extreme, but less so; that shrinkage toward the population average is the regression effect.[7]

Statistically, regression toward the mean arises whenever two measurements are imperfectly correlated: an unusually extreme value is partly the product of chance, and chance is not repeated. In the height case the parents' extreme stature reflects both inherited and non-inherited contributions, and only the inherited part is passed on, so the offspring distribution is centred closer to the population mean.[2] Wikipedia notes that the effect is descriptive rather than causal and that the term has since spread into general statistics far beyond genetics.[2]

The mid-parental height is the combined figure from both parents, adjusted for the child's sex. A child's final height is usually compared with a range around that target rather than a single number.[3]

Francis Galton arrived at the idea through experiments on the sizes of sweet-pea seeds in the 1870s, calling the pattern first reversion and later regression.[8] He presented the explanation in his 1885 presidential address to the British Association, and in 1886 published "Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature" in the Journal of the Anthropological Institute.[8][2]

For the stature study Galton used family records: heights of 930 adult children and of their 205 sets of parents. To avoid objections based on sex differences he multiplied every female height by 1.08 to convert it to a male equivalent, and he combined the two parents into a single "mid-parent" value.[1] Galton found that the average deviation of the offspring from the population mean was a constant fraction, about two-thirds, of the mid-parent's deviation.[2][1] His data came from his Anthropometric Laboratory and family-record collections, and the work fed into his Natural Inheritance (1889) and later the development of correlation and linear regression.[8][2]

Galton's own explanation was based on ancestry: a child inherits not only from its parents but from more remote ancestors, so extremes dilute over generations. Later genetics replaced that account, but the statistical result he measured, and the word regression, remained.[2]

The best-known clinical formula is attributed to Tanner and colleagues (1970): for boys, the father's height plus the mother's height plus 13 cm, divided by two; for girls, the same sum minus 13 cm, divided by two. The conventional range around the target is plus or minus 8.5 cm, roughly the 3rd to 97th percentile.[9][10] The 13 cm figure is the average adult sex difference, and a 2025 review notes that equivalent factors vary by population, for example 13.2 cm in the UK, 14.4 in Flanders and 15.8 in India.[9]

Several refinements exist. Tanner and Buckler suggested adjusting by 1 cm for every 5 cm that the mid-parental height departs from the population mean, to build in regression. Wright and colleagues expressed the target in standard-deviation scores as roughly half of the mid-parental score. Hermanussen and Cole (2002) proposed a sex-neutral formula multiplying the average parental score by 0.72, which accounts for the correlation between parents and for assortative mating; the 2025 BMC Pediatrics review recommends it and notes it is already used in growth-hormone treatment studies.[9] A Swedish formula by Luo and colleagues uses regression coefficients of about 0.75-0.78 on mid-parental height.[9]

A 2024 study from a team including Zeevi examined 23 large families and reported that children were on average 2.7 cm taller than the standard prediction, with the gap shrinking to roughly 0.06 cm after correcting parental heights for age; the authors proposed an age-corrected algorithm.[10]

Reviewers describe target height as an estimate, not an exact calculation.[9] The Tanner approach underestimates adult height in several modern populations, by about 2.3 cm in Taiwan and larger amounts in some Indian and Spanish samples, partly because it ignores secular trends: average height has risen by up to about 10 cm in industrialised countries over roughly 150 years.[9][7]

Because of regression, the plain formula tends to under-predict children of short parents and over-predict children of very tall parents.[9][10] Parental height correlation (assortative mating) of 0.1-0.4, and disparity between parents, also reduce accuracy.[9] Self-reported parental heights are often overestimated, by 4-6 cm or more, especially for fathers and short parents, which is why measured heights are preferred.[9]

Genetics is more complex than a single parental average. Twin studies put the heritability of height at about 60-80%, and genome-wide association studies have identified hundreds of variants in hundreds of loci, including groups that mainly influence leg length, spine and head length, or overall body size.[7] Nutrition and health in childhood also matter: malnutrition can reduce adult height, and diet quality is associated with differences between populations.[7]
Reviews of neonatal and postnatal growth state that expected growth should be predicted from mid-parental height, a step that is frequently omitted.[3]

In growth disorders, the target is a reference point. Gigantism is defined partly as height more than two standard deviations above mid-parental height, which leads to checks for excess growth hormone and related conditions.[4] In Klinefelter syndrome, adult height tends to exceed mid-parental height.[11] Short stature in children with severe atopic eczema has been defined as height below the third centile corrected for mid-parental height.[12] In short stature therapy, mid-parental height is one factor shaping how a child responds to growth hormone, alongside age at start and bone age; reviews of growth hormone receptor genetics also list it among the variables that partly explain individual response.[5][13]

Bone age and puberty timing are used alongside the parental target. The 2025 review reports that children with advanced bone age and no endocrine disorder usually finish within the target range, though they reach it earlier, and that pathological precocious or delayed puberty may leave adult height below it, with studies disagreeing.[9]

Height threads on looksmax.org frequently include parents' heights when users ask about their potential, for example a 17-year-old posting his own height and both parents' heights and asking what he could reach if growth plates are still open.[6] The target figure is used as a rough projection and compared with actual growth to judge whether to see an endocrinologist; some posters discuss growth hormone and aromatase inhibitors in this context, which are prescription medicines that clinicians manage for specific diagnoses.[5]

In these communities height is widely treated as a fixed, high-value trait, and the target calculation functions as the gateway concept: it frames what is genetic baseline and what, if anything, could be changed. Posters commonly pair it with bone-age X-rays, growth-plate status and stack-style routines for sleep, nutrition and training, while height-adding footwear and limb-lengthening surgery sit at the other end of the discussion as options that do not depend on the target.

Published reviews describe mid-parental height as a standard predictor in growth monitoring and treatment response.[3][5] Studies of specific conditions report how final height compares with the parental target, for example in Klinefelter syndrome.[11] The accuracy of the Tanner formula and its alternatives has been compared in population samples, with reported under-estimation in several countries and recommendations for sex-neutral or population-specific formulas.[9] A family-based cohort study has proposed an age-corrected version.[10] These are paediatric and statistical studies of the prediction itself rather than trials of an intervention.

lore.intro: On height forums, parents' heights are treated as the first clue to a person's potential, and the mid-parental target is quoted as a baseline that other factors may push up or down.[6]

timeline.event: Galton begins sweet-pea experiments on inheritance of seed size, the origin of his regression idea.[8]
Galton opens his Anthropometric Laboratory, collecting body measurements from thousands of visitors.[8]
Galton gives his British Association presidential address explaining the regression phenomenon.[8]
Galton publishes "Regression towards mediocrity in hereditary stature", using 930 adult children of 205 mid-parents.[1][2]
Natural Inheritance presents the idea alongside the Galton board and the Law of Ancestral Heredity.[2][8]
Tanner and colleagues' mid-parental target height formula and +/-8.5 cm range enters paediatric practice.[9]
Luo and colleagues publish a regression-based Swedish target-height formula from 2,402 children.[9]
Hermanussen and Cole propose a sex-neutral target-height formula built on a 0.72 factor.[9]
Zeevi and colleagues report an age-corrected target-height method from 23 large families.[10]
A BMC Pediatrics review assesses the accuracy of Tanner's formula across populations and recommends the Hermanussen-Cole approach.[9]
